A malediction is a curse — a deliberate, intentional spoken (or written) wish that evil, harm, or misfortune will befall a specific person. When someone delivers a malediction, they are not simply venting anger or using a bad word. They are actively and purposefully calling down ruin, suffering, or doom upon another person, often with a solemn, weighty, almost ceremonial sense of intent behind it.

Think of it this way: if someone snaps "I hope things go badly for you," that is a frustrated remark. But if someone looks you in the eye and solemnly declares "May sorrow shadow your every step, may your name be forgotten, and may everything you build crumble to dust" — that is a malediction.

It is not the same as swearing or insulting someone. This distinction is critical. Profanity is impulsive and emotional — it relieves frustration. An insult attacks your character or dignity. A malediction does something different entirely: it is a directed act, designed with the purpose of invoking harm upon you. It is a weapon made entirely of words, and it is always aimed.

Maledictions carry formality and gravity. This is not a casual, everyday word, and neither is the act it describes. In literature, mythology, and religious traditions across history, a malediction was often a serious, formal act — pronounced by a wronged king upon his betrayers, spoken by a scorned figure with perceived supernatural power, or declared by a religious authority as divine condemnation. The word carries that same heaviness whenever it appears. You will never hear someone use "malediction" lightly.

How intense can a malediction be? It exists on a spectrum. At the milder end, it can refer to a fierce, formal verbal condemnation — a solemn denunciation of someone using words alone, with no supernatural element implied. At its most intense, and most common, it refers to a supernatural curse — a spoken invocation of evil that the speaker, the culture, or the fictional world genuinely believes to carry power. Both uses are valid, and context will usually make clear which is meant.

Here are some clear examples of the word in action:

"The scorned elder rose and spoke a malediction against the village that had cast her out, vowing that misfortune would poison it for generations."

"Carved into the chamber wall was a malediction in an ancient tongue, warning that any who entered would carry its curse to their grave."

"His parting words to the court were not a farewell but a malediction — he cursed every man who had voted against him."

Its perfect opposite is "benediction," and understanding this contrast makes the word click into place instantly. A benediction is a blessing — a formal, spoken wish for someone's wellbeing, grace, and good fortune. A priest gives a benediction at the close of a ceremony. A malediction is the dark mirror image of that: a formal, spoken wish for someone's suffering and destruction. Where a benediction uplifts, a malediction strikes down. They are structurally the same act — a solemn, intentional utterance directed at a person — but one gives and the other destroys.

Where will you encounter this word? Most commonly in literary fiction (especially fantasy, gothic, and historical fiction), mythology, religious texts, and elevated non-fiction. When you come across it, you can be certain it signals a curse — one with deliberateness, weight, and often a formal or ritualistic quality to it.

When should you use it yourself? Reserve it for serious, elevated writing. It would feel theatrical and out of place in casual speech, but in writing — especially when you want to convey that a curse is not just a throwaway angry comment but a purposeful, weighty act of wishing evil — malediction is the precise and powerful word to reach for. It says everything that "curse" says, and adds the gravity, formality, and intentionality that makes the act feel truly dangerous.
